items.titleEn: Gold, silver advance as dollar weakens, Fed rate expectations face inflation test - Kitco PM Report
items.summaryEn: (Kitco NewsWire) - Spot gold and silver prices were sharply higher in late U.S. trading Monday, supported by a weaker U.S. dollar and a steep decline in crude oil prices as investors responded to renewed hopes for a diplomatic resolution to the U.S.-Iran conflict. The retreat in energy prices eased some inflation concerns ahead of Tuesday's U.S. consumer price index report, although Friday's stronger-than-expected employment figures continued to support expectations for another Federal Reserve interest rate increase in December. A broad recovery in North American and European equity markets also reflected improving investor sentiment following last week's technology-led selloff. Spot gold was trading near $4,140.40 an ounce, up $69.40, or 1.70%, while spot silver was trading near $53.320, up $1.350, or 2.60%. Gold extended its recovery following last week's sharp fluctuations, when Democrats' victories in the U.S. midterm elections initially drove Treasury yields and the dollar lower before stronger employment data revived expectations for additional Federal Reserve tightening. Monday's decline in crude oil prices helped offset some of those monetary policy concerns, while the softer dollar improved the relative attractiveness of precious metals. Silver outperformed gold as the recovery in broader financial markets encouraged renewed buying interest. The latest U.S. economic reports continue to indicate resilient labor-market conditions despite elevated borrowing costs and recent volatility in technology shares. Friday's October nonfarm payrolls report showed an increase of 165,000 jobs, substantially exceeding expectations for approximately 65,000. The unemployment rate declined to 4.1% from 4.2%, while average hourly earnings increased 0.4% on the month and 3.1% annually. August and September payroll figures were revised upward by a combined 84,000 jobs, reinforcing evidence that employment conditions remain stronger than previously estimated. The figures increased expectations that the Fed could raise interest rates again in December, even as financial-market volatility and declining energy prices complicate the inflation outlook.
